name: BEAM.com (Erlang/OTP + Elixir single Cosmopolitan binary)
baseline: beam-emu.com, the same repository's own interpreter-only build (BeamAsm JIT off); no comparison against stock Erlang/OTP is published
workload: tests/bench/bench.erl run with the JIT build (beam.com) and the interpreter build (beam-emu.com): fib(32), lists:sort/map/foldl on 1,000,000 numbers, 200,000 map and ETS inserts and lookups, 5 MB binary match, 200,000 messages, startup time; best of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: JIT build against the repo's own interpreter build, CI Linux x86_64 (ms, interpreter -> JIT): fib 70 -> 30, lists 249 -> 116, binary 249 -> 133, maps 83 -> 68, ets 70 -> 64, messages 111 -> 117; Linux aarch64: fib 139 -> 12, lists 411 -> 104, binary 290 -> 91; startup is slower with the JIT (--version 142 -> 222 ms on Linux x86_64). Stored kernel/stdlib zip entries cut start of beam.com --version from 193-202 ms to 143-146 ms (local, own earlier variant). No number against stock Erlang/OTP.
hardware: CI runners (shared machines) and a local Linux x86_64 box with 4 CPUs; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Packaging of the unmodified Erlang/OTP 29 ERTS and Elixir 1.20 as one Actually Portable Executable (Cosmopolitan Libc, about 50 MB, also a zip with the OTP applications); runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD on x86_64 and aarch64; includes OpenSSL, SQLite and WAMR. The JIT adds 2.8 MB and 40 to 90 ms of start time. A second runtime (ERTS compiled to WebAssembly) runs on Cloudflare Workers and Deno Deploy at 1.2 to 1.4 times the time of the native interpreter in Node.js (WORKERS.md, October 2026).
caveats: Nothing in the repo shows BEAM.com beating stock Erlang/OTP. The BeamAsm JIT it ships is the one stock OTP already has on x86_64 and aarch64, so the fib 2x to 12x gains are JIT against interpreter, not against the incumbent BEAM. Its own measurements are first-party, from shared CI machines with noise it states as about 10%, with no CPU model or compiler flags, and the gate tables carry only relative limits. The only quantity that is faster by design is the packaging (one portable file, stored kernel and stdlib start about 27% faster than its own all-compressed variant). Kept as tier D because no recognizable baseline is beaten.

name: TinyKVM (Varnish KVM sandbox; per-request numbers come from libriscv/kvmserver)
baseline: per-request sandboxing by process fork, a new V8 isolate or WebAssembly-embedded interpreters (the alternatives the benchmark page names); native Linux process as the speed reference. Wasmtime and WAMR are not compared on any page opened
workload: kvmserver (separate repo built on TinyKVM) runs unmodified Linux server executables with a TinyKVM VM reset after each request: Rust minimal HTTP server, Deno hello world and Deno React page rendering; 1000 warmup requests, load generator against native, kvmserver and kvmserver ephemeral.
claimed_speedup: Page claim: 'We are able to run this benchmark 1.5-2 orders of magnitude faster than existing solutions' (previous React experiments: 'runtimes in the 10s of milliseconds with WebAssembly' and 'reset times of several milliseconds' for process fork or a new V8 isolate), against 55 us sandbox reset and 80 us total per-request overhead out of 690 us on the React benchmark. Against native it is slower: React page 646 us native vs 695 us ephemeral kvmserver (threads=1); Rust minimal server 13 us native vs 28 us; Deno hello world 17 us vs 50 us.
compiler_and_flags: Deno 2.3.6 run with --v8-flags=--predictable and built with deno compile; Rust server build flags not stated; TinyKVM build flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 823 stars; used by Varnish (VMOD-TinyKVM) and libriscv/kvmserver
tradeoffs: Needs /dev/kvm and Linux KVM (x86-64, with an arm64 feature matrix in docs); runs ordinary Linux programs at near-native speed with execution timeouts, memory limits and fork of an initialised program into many pre-initialised VMs. Syscalls needing the host cost about 1 us each; nested virtualization adds about 200 us; reset time grows with dirty pages and open file descriptors. Dual licence: GPL-3.0 or a commercial licence from Varnish Software.
caveats: The varnish/tinykvm README and docs carry no benchmark, only the qualitative 'run it in TinyKVM at the same speed' claim, and tests/ has no benchmarks. The numbers above are from libriscv/kvmserver, a separate project from the same author, and measure kvmserver plus TinyKVM, not TinyKVM alone. The fork, V8 isolate and WebAssembly baseline figures are described as 'previous experiments' with no table, so the 1.5-2 orders of magnitude claim is not reproducible from the page. Per request it is slower than native. Search snippets (Hacker News comment and a Medium post, neither openable here, snippet only) mention 2.5 us snapshot restore 'on par with Wasmtime' and about 14 us end-to-end per request; they were not used as evidence.

name: ncruces/wasm2go (Wasm to Go compiler)
baseline: wazero (WebAssembly runtime for Go; version and execution mode not stated)
workload: pgaskin/go-marisa BenchmarkTrie (a WebAssembly build of the MARISA trie called from Go, Words and Go125 datasets): build, ReadFrom, WriteTo, marshal and unmarshal, lookup, reverse lookup, predictive and common-prefix search; wazero-bound build against wasm2go-transpiled build, benchstat of 6 runs.
claimed_speedup: benchstat sec/op, wasm2go against wazero: geomean 109.5us -> 92.58us (-15.45%); Trie/Go125/Lookup 96.77ns -> 70.31ns (-27.34%); Trie/Words/ReverseLookup 123.65ns -> 73.63ns (-40.45%); Trie/Words/Lookup 344.2ns -> 306.8ns (-10.87%); Trie/Words/WriteTo 11.383us -> 2.541us (-77.68%); CommonPrefixSearchSeq -12% to -18%. Slower: Trie/Words/Build 349.4ms -> 406.9ms (+16.46%), Trie/Go125/Build +34.67%, Trie/Words/UnmarshalBinary 323.6us -> 634.8us (+96.16%). Keys/s geomean 2.525M -> 2.802M (+10.97%).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 (go1.26.0): CGO_ENABLED=0 go test -v -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkTrie -count=6 github.com/pgaskin/go-marisa; wasm2go commit 075b64a04783d6c188ac9f66ea52688bc71edb9e; wazero version not stated
hardware: Lenovo T14s Gen 6, Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7 258V (linux/amd64, 8 threads), performance mode
stars_or_usage: 237 stars; adopted by ncruces/go-sqlite3 and pgaskin/go-marisa
tradeoffs: Translates a Wasm module to self-contained Go source with no dependencies beyond Go, so no runtime and no cgo; the output is deliberately unreadable (goto labels, type conversions) and its speed depends on the Go compiler's assembly. A static translation: runtime loading of arbitrary modules still needs wazero (stated in the discussion). Large generated files cost compile time and memory (a commenter in discussion #361 reported about 40 seconds and 4 GB of RAM to compile). Each module instance keeps its own memory up to 4 GB.
caveats: Mixed result on one workload and one machine: queries and WriteTo are faster, build and some read paths are slower, so the geomean win (-15.45%) hides regressions up to +96%. Run by pgaskin (the go-marisa author) rather than the wasm2go author, which makes it independent, but the wazero version and the flags used to build the MARISA Wasm blob are not stated; go-marisa's README summarises the same switch as 'slightly faster at querying, but about 50% slower at building/reading/writing'. Not the go-sqlite3 workload that the discussion is about. Separate project from goccy/wasm2go.

name: FEX (x86/x86-64 emulator for ARM64 with JIT)
baseline: QEMU user-mode (qemu-x86_64 and qemu-i386); Box64 is faster than FEX in the same tables
workload: 7-Zip benchmark (MIPS), dav1d (1 and 4 threads), glmark2 and OpenArena run as x86 and x86_64 binaries under QEMU user-mode, FEX and Box64 on an ARM Linux machine, by the Box86/Box64 author in March 2022.
claimed_speedup: x86_64 guest, FEX against QEMU: 7z 1486 vs 931 (1.6x, derived from page data); dav1d 1 thread 27.28 vs 11.24 (2.4x, derived from page data); dav1d 4 threads 52.67 vs 15.65 (3.4x, derived from page data); glmark2 164 vs 4; OpenArena 1.8 vs 0.083. x86 guest: 7z 1197 vs 691, dav1d 1 thread 21.75 vs 10.57. Box64 in the same table: 7z 3084, dav1d 1 thread 49.72, glmark2 178, OpenArena 8.4.
stars_or_usage: 8.2k stars; integrated by Android game runners per repo discussion #4113
tradeoffs: ARM64 Linux host only; x86 and x86-64 guests via a binary recompiler with a custom IR; forwards API calls to host libraries (thunking); per-app configuration and an experimental code cache; GUI configuration tool. Not supported on Android.
caveats: Snippet only: box86.org is blocked here, so the table was read from search-result text, and the CPU model, compiler flags and QEMU and FEX versions are not visible. The measurement is from March 2022 and was made by the Box86/Box64 author, a competing project; FEX has changed a lot since, and its maintainer said in October 2024 (discussion #4113) that FEX has no comparison against Box and that CPU emulation performance has improved over time. FEX publishes no numbers of its own against QEMU in the README, and its wiki and site were not reachable. In these tables FEX is slower than Box64 on every row.

name: dstogov/ir (IR framework and JIT behind PHP 8.4+ JIT)
baseline: gcc -O2 (compile time; the README also reports the generated code speed against it)
workload: 18 programs (14 small benchmarks such as binary-trees, mandelbrot, nbody, hash, sieve plus oggenc, minilua, gzip, bzip2) compiled by clang to LLVM IR without LLVM optimization and then loaded, compiled and run by IR, against the same programs built by gcc -O2; compile time is reported for the four real applications.
claimed_speedup: Compile time relative to gcc -O2: oggenc 35.22, minilua 40.50, gzip 37.50, bzip2 49.67, average 40.69, geomean 40.34 ('IR framework provides code that is in average 5% slower, but does this up to ~40 times faster'). Generated code speed relative to gcc -O2: average and geomean 0.96, worst gzip 0.80 and bzip2 0.81, best hash 1.13 and matrix 1.12.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O2 (version not stated); inputs lowered by clang to LLVM IR with no LLVM optimizations (README example: clang -O -Xclang -disable-llvm-passes -c -emit-llvm -S); IR build flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 507 stars; the JIT backend of PHP 8.4 and later
tradeoffs: Lightweight graph-based SSA IR with APIs for construction, optimization passes, scheduling, register allocation and code generation; optional LLVM interop (convert IR to and from LLVM IR); also used as the backend of the experimental Rational C Compiler. Generates code on average about 4 to 5% slower than gcc -O2, up to about 20% slower in the worst case.
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model, no compiler versions and no run script: bench/ in the repo holds only mandelbrot.c, mandelbrot.ir and mandelbrot.lua, so the tables are not reproducible from the repo. The README itself says the compile-time comparison 'is not completely fair' because gcc compiles C source while IR consumes precompiled LLVM IR, which leaves out the front-end. The win is compile time only; code quality is below gcc -O2 on average. The table header says 'Execution time ... (the more the better)', which is ambiguous, but the prose ('5% slower, ~20% slower in the worst case') and the 0.80 to 1.13 range read as speed relative to gcc. No LLVM compile-time comparison is on the page. The chart is hosted on dstogov.github.io and was not opened.

name: TurboPython / tpy (typed Python to C++ without GC)
baseline: CPython (Shed Skin, Cython, mypyc, Nuitka and Codon appear in the README only as design contrasts, with no timings)
workload: None published: no benchmark against CPython, Shed Skin or Cython in the README, RELEASE_NOTES.md, TODO.md or the examples repo; the only timing script is scripts/perf/generator_frames.py, which compares generator forms inside tpy.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. The README says the output has no interpreter, no garbage collector, no reference counting and no GIL.
tradeoffs: Statically typed Python compiled through C++ (g++ 13+ or clang++ 19+) to a native binary; deterministic ownership model (Own[T], Rc, Arc[Mutex[T]]) instead of GC or reference counting; not a drop-in CPython replacement and no CPython packages (everything imported is TurboPython source, with a CPython extension-module export mode); Linux and macOS, WSL on Windows; standard library is a subset.
caveats: Early development, pre-1.0: the README says 'known bugs can produce wrong results silently' and BUGS.md lists many open items. No speed evidence at all, so tier D with very low notability (6 stars). TODO.md records one internal measurement (generator frames, gcc-14 and clang-20, default -O3, ms per 50 x 2M elements) that compares tpy generator forms with each other, not with CPython. Name collision: the PyPI package 'turbopython' is a different project (ribalba/TurboPython, version 0.1.0, March 2026) whose README claims 37.1x (Mandelbrot) and 59.4x (Fibonacci) over pure Python; those numbers do not belong to trozen/tpy-lang.

name: EOS VM Optimized Compiler (eosvmoc in AntelopeIO/spring)
baseline: EOS VM JIT and EOS VM interpreter (also WABT and Binaryen per the docs claim; WAVM is the origin of the code)
workload: Execution of WebAssembly smart contracts in an Antelope node: an LLVM-based tier that compiles a contract in the background while the baseline runtime (EOS VM JIT) serves it, then switches to the optimized native code.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in spring. A search snippet of the EOS VM documentation (snippet only) says native code from the optimized compiler is 'often an order of magnitude faster' than the same code in WABT, Binaryen, the EOS VM interpreter and the EOS VM JIT.
stars_or_usage: 30 stars; runs the Antelope/EOS blockchain node (Spring, formerly Leap)
tradeoffs: x86_64 Linux only; needs LLVM; has compile_monitor, compile_trampoline and code_cache components and a tier-up design so the first calls run on the baseline runtime; a leap issue is titled 'Reduce EOS VM OC's memory slice count allowing for higher parallelization' (seen in search results only); code created in part from WAVM, and the eos-vm-oc files carry WAVM's BSD-3-Clause notice (spring's top-level LICENSE is MIT).
caveats: spring has no benchmark for the OC tier: the repo has no README or docs for eos-vm-oc (only an 'About WAVM' note), and the spring README has no performance numbers. The 'order of magnitude' claim comes from a search-result snippet of the EOS VM docs (eos.io page could not be opened, host unresolvable) with no workload, hardware or compiler. Tier D by the assignment rule; the eos-vm repo is catalogued separately. Last commit date is from the commits page of main (Nov 2025); the releases page shows v2.0.0-dev1.3 on 27 Aug (year not displayed), so work may continue on release branches.
